en: Sutta Nipāta 2.5 Sūcilomasutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Gayā, on the Ṭaṅkitamañca, in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma.
Now at that time, the yakkhas Kharo and Sūciloma were passing by not far from the Blessed One.
Then the yakkha Kharo said this to the yakkha Sūciloma:
“This is an ascetic.
“This is not an ascetic; this is a mere pseudo-ascetic.
I shall first find out whether he is truly an ascetic or merely a pseudo-ascetic.”
Then the yakkha Sūciloma approached the Blessed One; having approached, he thrust his body toward the Blessed One’s body.
Then the Blessed One withdrew his body.
Thereupon the yakkha Sūciloma said this to the Blessed One:
“Are you afraid of me, ascetic?
“I am not afraid of you, friend;
however, your touch is evil.”
“I will ask you a question, ascetic.
If you do not answer me, I will either strike at your mind, or split your heart, or else seize you by the feet and hurl you across the Ganges.
“Friend, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—”
"In this world with its devas and humans, he could throw my mind into confusion, or split my heart,
or seize me by the feet and cast me across the Ganges.
Nevertheless, friend, ask whatever you wish."
Then the yakkha Sūciloma addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“From what source do passion and hatred arise?
From where do discontent, delight, and horripilation spring?”
“From what do mental thoughts arise,
like young birds releasing from a hawk?
“Lust and hatred have their source from this.”
Dislike, delight, and horripilation are born from this;
mental thoughts arising from this dart forth like young birds from a hawk.
Born of affection, sprung from oneself,
like the trunks of a banyan tree;
they are widely entangled in sensual pleasures.
In this forest spread with māluvā creepers,
those who understand its origin,
O yakkha, dispel it; listen!
They cross this flood so difficult to cross,
which was never crossed before, so as to reach the state of no further becoming.
Thus ends the fifth discourse, the Sūciloma Sutta.
